tier_reason: Public benchmark code in gnet-io/gnet-benchmarks (bench-echo.sh driving tcpkali against echo-gnet-server/main.go and echo-net-server/main.go), with compiler (go1.17.2 linux/amd64), build flags in bench-echo.sh (go build -gcflags="-l=4" -ldflags="-s -w", plus -tags=poll_opt for gnet) and CPU (8 cores of AMD EPYC 7K62) all stated. The chart values are backed by raw tcpkali logs in results/echo_linux.txt.

corrections.baseline: Go standard library net package (runtime netpoller over epoll)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Echo benchmark, 1KB packet, Linux: gnet had the highest QPS (tcpkali packet-rate estimate) at every connection count vs. Go std net: 1000 conns 4,646,164 vs 3,250,189 (~1.43x); 2000 conns 4,374,275 vs 2,371,727 (~1.84x); 5000 conns 3,191,612 vs 2,285,845 (~1.40x); 10000 conns 2,619,695 vs 1,343,247 (~1.95x) (ratios derived from page data)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: go1.17.2 linux/amd64; go build -gcflags="-l=4" -ldflags="-s -w" for all servers, plus -tags=poll_opt for gnet (bench-echo.sh); GOMAXPROCS=8; gnet v1.5.3 per go.mod at the chart commit
corrections.stars_or_usage: 11,251 stars; the README's use-case list names Tencent, Tencent Games, iQIYI, Xiaomi, 360, Baidu Tieba, JD, Zuoyebang and ByteDance as production users
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from a chart committed Oct 2021 (backed by raw tcpkali logs in results/echo_linux.txt) in gnet-io/gnet-benchmarks (39 stars, last commit Dec 2024). It measured gnet v1.5.3 on Go 1.17.2, not current gnet v2 or newer Go netpollers. Both gnet and Go net use epoll underneath, so the real baseline is Go's std net, not epoll itself. The QPS values are tcpkali packet-rate estimates over localhost with 8 cores. A companion TechEmpower Round 22 plaintext claim (gnet ranked #1 of 486) is chart-only in the README, and the README admits gnet's TechEmpower HTTP code is benchmark-tuned and not production-ready.

notes: Chart numbers match the record exactly. The record's claim that gnet powers ByteDance's Kitex and Hertz is false: both depend on cloudwego/netpoll according to their go.mod files. ByteDance is only listed as a gnet user in the README. Baseline was changed from epoll to Go std net because gnet itself is epoll-based.

tier_reason: This is the libev author's own writeup. The benchmark code is public (http://libev.schmorp.de/bench.c, a modified copy of libevent's bench.c), and the compiler and flags are stated (gcc 4.2.3 -O3 -fno-guess-branch-probability -g). The CPU, however, is given only as 'a Core2 Quad at 3.6GHz', a family and clock with no model or SKU, so it misses A. First-party with partial methodology is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: libev 3.31 vs libevent 1.4.3 (both on epoll) using libevent's bench.c. With no timeouts, libevent takes 'almost twice as much time than libev' in total time per iteration (the gap grows with fd count), but the event-processing (poll) times differ by less than 5%. With per-connection idle timeouts, libev's event processing is 'consistently faster (with a factor of two to almost three)' over 100-100,000 fds, and overall time 'has been almost halved'. The 2011 appendix rerun (libev 4.03 vs libevent 1.4.13 and 2.0.10) shows the same pattern. All figures are from the page's prose; the charts carry no numeric tables.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1,790 stars on the unofficial GitHub mirror (enki/libev). Node.js bundled it through v0.4 (deps/libev). The upstream page lists GNU Virtual Private Ethernet, rxvt-unicode, auditd and the Deliantra server and client as users.
corrections.caveats: enki/libev is an unofficial GitHub mirror stuck at libev 4.22 (Dec 2015). Upstream lives in schmorpforge CVS (http://software.schmorp.de/pkg/libev.html), and its latest release, 4.33, is from 2020-03-18. The benchmark is the libev author's own: the original run (libevent 1.4.3 vs libev 3.31) is from ~2008 and the writeup was last revised 2011-01-11 (version 6). The CPU is given only as 'Core2 Quad at 3.6GHz', and results are line charts, not tables. Without timeouts, the gain is almost entirely in watcher setup; poll times are within 5%. libuv is not covered. The independent bartman/event-loop-benchmark (5 stars, -Os -ggdb, no hardware stated) reuses this bench.c. In its README, libev's total is ~27.5k µs vs libevent's ~123k µs, but libevent's event-processing column is lower (~215 vs ~270 µs).

notes: The numbers and prose match the page. Downgraded from A to C because the CPU is given only by family and clock (no model) and the benchmark is first-party; this follows earlier batches' rulings on family-only CPUs. The record's usage claims 'EventMachine, Tor' could not be verified and look wrong (Tor uses libevent, and EventMachine has its own reactor), so they were replaced with verified users.

tier_reason: First-party README (copied from the author's 2009 Cybozu Labs post) with two charts, 'Setup Time (1,000 active)' and 'Event Processing Time (1,000 active)', plotting picoev against libevent and libev (emul and native). The benchmark code is public (example/bench.c, a modified libevent/libev bench.c), but no compiler, flags, CPU or library versions are stated, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'it is faster than libevent or libev!' The two charts (1,000 active clients, 1k-100k fds) show picoev lowest throughout. At 100,000 fds, setup time is about 600k µs for libevent vs about 190k µs for picoev (~3x), and event-processing time is about 22.5k vs about 11k µs (~2x). libev (native) is close behind picoev (~12k µs). These values are approximate, read off the unlabeled chart axes (derived from page data).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 403 stars; vendored by the meinheld Python WSGI server (meinheld/server/picoev_*.c, ~1.45k stars)
corrections.caveats: There is no LICENSE file. The BSD-3-Clause terms come from per-file headers (Copyright 2009 Cybozu Labs, with an unfilled '<ORGANIZATION>' placeholder), and the 326-byte declarations-only picoev_w32.h has no header. The README's chart images and original post on developer.cybozu.co.jp are dead; they survive only on web.archive.org (picoev_setup.png and picoev_event.png, 2015 snapshots). The charts have no numeric labels, and there is no stated compiler, flags, hardware, library versions or timeout settings. Only select, epoll and kqueue backends are supported, and timeouts have coarse 1-second granularity (a 128-slot ring of bit vectors). In the independent bartman/event-loop-benchmark README (5 stars, -Os -ggdb, picoev built -O2, no hardware stated), picoev's total is ~61k µs vs libevent's ~123k µs per run, with libev fastest at ~27.5k µs.

notes: The claim is qualitative in the README, and the archived charts support it against both libevent and libev. The record's 'license: null' was wrong: every core source file has a BSD-3-Clause header, so usability becomes copyable. Tier C is unchanged.
